lesson.title: Confirmation Bias: Seeing What You Expect to See
lesson.summary: This section explains confirmation bias ,  the tendency to favor information that fits existing beliefs ,  and shows how it distorted decision-making during the Vietnam War and continues to shape how historians read evidence.
lesson.body:
You already know that a cognitive bias is a systematic mental shortcut that can distort judgment without the person noticing. Confirmation bias is one of the most powerful of these shortcuts, and it works through three connected habits: seeking out information that supports what you already believe, interpreting ambiguous information in a way that fits your existing view, and remembering the evidence that confirmed you were right more easily than the evidence that suggested you were wrong. None of this requires dishonesty. It happens because holding a consistent picture of the world feels more comfortable and less mentally taxing than constantly questioning it, so the mind quietly favors the path that avoids that discomfort.

The mechanism matters more than the label. Imagine someone convinced that a particular policy is working well. When new reports come in, they don't evaluate every piece of evidence with equal weight ,  they read the encouraging report closely and accept it at face value, while they skim the discouraging report, look for reasons to doubt its methodology, or assume it's an outlier. Over time, this creates an asymmetry: confirming evidence gets absorbed easily, disconfirming evidence gets filtered out or reinterpreted. The person isn't lying to themselves on purpose; they simply apply a different, harsher standard of scrutiny to information that threatens their existing belief than to information that supports it.

This bias becomes especially dangerous when it operates inside an entire information system, not just one person's head. During the Vietnam War, President Lyndon Johnson relied on daily intelligence briefings assembled by military and civilian advisors. Those advisors understood, consciously or not, what kind of news Johnson wanted to hear about the war's progress. As a result, the briefings tended to emphasize signs of success and downplay signs of failure, long before they ever reached the president's desk. Johnson wasn't simply a victim of his own confirmation bias in reading the reports ,  the bias had already shaped which facts made it into the reports at all. This shows you an important extension of the concept: confirmation bias can be built into an organization's structure, where subordinates filter information upward to please superiors, producing a feedback loop that grows more distorted the longer it continues.

Confirmation bias also affects how historians study the past, which is why it belongs in a skills-focused chapter rather than only a psychology one. A historian who begins research already convinced that a particular figure was heroic, or that a particular policy caused a specific outcome, faces the same temptation Johnson's advisors faced: sources that support the thesis feel more compelling and get quoted more often, while sources that complicate or contradict it get labeled as unreliable, unrepresentative, or beside the point. This doesn't mean historians can never form conclusions ,  it means good historical practice requires deliberately searching for the strongest evidence against your own interpretation before deciding you're right, rather than stopping once you've found evidence that agrees with you.

Recognizing confirmation bias, then, is not just about noticing it in long-dead policymakers. It's a habit of mind you can apply to any historical claim, including your own: ask whether you sought out disconfirming evidence as actively as you sought out confirming evidence, and whether you're judging a source's reliability by its quality or by whether you like its conclusion.
